stem:
Four diodes are used in a bridge rectifier circuit to produce rectification of a sinusoidal a.c. input voltage *V*ᵢₙ.
Fig. 7.1 shows part of the circuit, but three of the diodes are missing.

[[fig:f1]]

The p.d. across the load resistor R is the output p.d. *V*ₒᵤₜ of the bridge rectifier.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State the name of the type of rectification produced by a bridge rectifier.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Complete Fig. 7.1 by drawing the three missing diodes, correctly connected.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: On Fig. 7.1, draw an arrow to indicate the direction of the current in resistor R.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.lead:
*V*ᵢₙ has amplitude *V*₀ and period *T*. Fig. 7.2 shows the variation with time *t* of *V*ᵢₙ.

[[fig:f2]]
parts.text: On Fig. 7.3, sketch the variation of *V*ₒᵤₜ with *t* between *t* = 0 and *t* = 2.0*T*.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The power dissipated in the resistor is *P*.

On Fig. 7.4, sketch the variation of *P* with *t* between *t* = 0 and *t* = 2.0*T*.

[[fig:f3]]

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, how the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of *V*ₒᵤₜ compares with the r.m.s. value of *V*ᵢₙ.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.1
figures.alt: A partially shown bridge rectifier circuit with an a.c. input, load resistor R, output voltage, and one diode drawn.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.2
figures.alt: A gridded graph showing the sinusoidal input voltage against time from 0 to 2.0T.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.3
figures.alt: A blank gridded graph for output voltage against time from 0 to 2.0T, marked with V₀ and −V₀.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.4
figures.alt: A blank gridded graph for power against time from 0 to 2.0T.
